meaning: because, since (formal written cause: reports, notices, rules, academic prose)
nuance: A neutral, logical "because" at home in writing: notices, contracts, reports, papers. In casual talk it sounds stilted; speech uses -(으)니까 or -아/어서. Unlike -아/어서 it takes past tense freely (끝났으므로). Formal notices can follow it with a polite instruction (위험하므로 들어가지 마십시오). ㄹ-stems keep the ㄹ (멀므로), and irregular stems change before 으 (미끄러우므로, 나으므로). Don't confuse it with -(으)ㅁ으로(써), nominalizer + particle, which means "by doing": 노력하므로 = because one tries; 노력함으로써 = by trying. See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 103.

contrasts.note: -기에 also gives grounds in writing, but it often frames why the speaker acted or judged a certain way and sounds more narrative; -(으)므로 is the neutral "since/therefore" of reports.
-(으)니만큼 adds "so it is only fitting"; -(으)므로 just states the cause.
-(으)ㅁ으로써 (by doing) looks similar on the page but marks a means, not a reason.

meaning: it is/does … (I grant that much), but …: concedes one point with contrastive focus
nuance: Here 는 puts contrastive focus on the predicate itself: the speaker grants exactly this much and no more, so a -지만/-는데 clause or an unspoken reservation follows. Tense and usually the honorific go on 하다, not on the stem: 가기는 했다 (갔기는 했다 is rarely heard and sounds off). The same contrastive 는 attaches inside other complex predicates: 먹어는 봤다 (I have tried it, at least), 좋지는 않다, 가 보지는 못했다. In speech -기는 contracts to -긴. See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 104.

contrasts.note: -기는커녕 denies the first point ("far from …"); -기는 하다 grants it before adding a "but".
-(으)ㄹ뿐더러 stacks two points pulling the same way; -기는 하다 sets up a point against the first.

meaning: whether … or …; no matter (what/who/how) … (the choice makes no difference)
nuance: Lists alternatives (A-든지 B-든지, often A-든지 말든지) or pairs with a question word (뭘 하든지, 어디에 가든지) to say the choice doesn't matter; 간에 or 상관없이 can follow for emphasis. Speech often shortens it to -든 (뭘 하든). After nouns: vowel 든지, consonant 이든지. The classic spelling trap: -든지 (choice) vs -던지 (retrospective, as in 얼마나 춥던지 "it was so cold that"). A command or suggestion can follow (가든지 말든지 마음대로 해). See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 106.

contrasts.note: -더라도 concedes a single (often hypothetical) fact; -든지 is indifference across alternatives.
N(이)라도 offers one second-best option; N(이)든지 says any of the options will do.
The retrospective -던 family (-던지, -던가) is a different ending; mixing up 든/던 is a common spelling error.

meaning: had …; used to … (a past situation that no longer holds, or one set further back in the past)
nuance: Korean has no obligatory past perfect. -았/었었- signals discontinuity: the past situation is over or reversed, or it lies further back than another past point. 서울에 살았다 just reports; 서울에 살았었다 implies you don't live there now. With one-off events whose result normally persists, it suggests the result was undone: 결혼했다 (and still married) vs 결혼했었다 (no longer). Translators often overuse it for English "had + past participle". When the English past perfect only marks sequence, plain -았/었다 is usually better Korean. See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 108.

contrasts.note: The modifier -았/었던 also points to a closed-off past, but inside a noun phrase (살았던 집).
-곤 했다 means "used to" for repeated episodes; -았/었었다 marks a state or event as over, repeated or not.

meaning: it seems …; I guess … (an inference from something the speaker has just noticed)
nuance: Draws a conclusion from evidence in front of the speaker: the lights are off, so 다들 자나 봐요. Verbs and 있다/없다 take -나 (or the more formal -는가); adjectives take -(으)ㄴ가 (바쁜가 봐요). 바쁘나 봐요 is common in casual speech but nonstandard. With yourself as subject it sounds like discovering something about yourself (제가 요즘 좀 피곤한가 봐요), which is fine but marked. It doesn't state what you already know, and it isn't used for evidence-free predictions; that is -(으)ㄹ 것 같다 or -(으)ㄹ걸요. -(으)ㄴ/는 것 같다 covers both inference and opinion and is softer. See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 109.

contrasts.note: -(으)ㄹ걸요 is a confident guess, often from background knowledge rather than fresh evidence.
-(으)ㄹ 리가 없다 rules a possibility out; -나 보다 leans toward it.
-더라 reports what you actually saw; -나 보다 infers from clues.

meaning: (1) at least, even if only (a second-best option); (2) with question words: any … at all; (3) V-아/어서라도: even if it means …-ing
nuance: Offers something as an acceptable fallback: 커피라도 마실래요? ("at least some coffee?"), which is softer and more modest than a plain object. Vowel 라도, consonant 이라도. With question words it means "any … at all" (누구라도, 언제라도), close to 누구든지. After a verb, -아/어서라도 shows willingness to go to lengths: 빚을 내서라도. Compare N이나, which can sound offhand or dismissive (커피나 마시자). 지금이라도 is a fixed "even now (better late than never)". See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 111.

contrasts.note: -더라도 concedes a whole clause ("even if …"); N(이)라도 works on a noun or, as -아/어서라도, on the means.
N(이)든지 says any option will do; N(이)라도 offers one modest option.

cloze.en: If you're busy on the weekend, let's meet briefly on a weekday evening at least.
It's late, but I'd like to come and pay my respects even now.

nearMiss.hint: After a consonant: 지금이라도.

nuance.situation: 손님이 왔는데 대접할 게 별로 없어요. 겸손하게 권하려면? (You have little to offer a guest.)

options.why: -(이)라도 offers tea as a modest stand-in: "at least some tea".
-까지 means "even, on top of everything", so it oversells the tea instead of downplaying it.
-도 ("also") implies something else was already offered; it lacks the modest "at least".

nuance.situation: "돈을 빌려야 하더라도 꼭 갈 거야"라는 뜻으로 말하려면? (You'll go even if you have to borrow money.)

options.why: -아/어서라도 = even if it takes that means.
-기라도 needs 하다 after it (빌리기라도 해서); as written the clause has no predicate.

meaning: tends to …; is on the … side; is fairly … (a hedged, relative judgment)
nuance: Places a claim on a scale ("rather", "relatively"), which makes it modest. It's typical for describing yourself or your habits. Verbs usually need a degree word or a scale (잘, 많이, 자주, 일찍, 빨리): 많이 먹는 편이다 is natural; 밥을 먹는 편이다 has nothing to measure. For one completed event, V-(으)ㄴ 편이다 rates it (시험을 잘 본 편이다 = did fairly well). For a past habit or state, the tense goes on 이다 (빠지는 편이었다). Rarely used for absolute facts. See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 112.

contrasts.note: -곤 하다 describes repeated episodes; -는 편이다 rates a general tendency.
-(으)ㄴ/는 셈이다 sums up what something amounts to; -는 편이다 hedges a trait or tendency.

examples.ko: 저는 아침을 꼭 챙겨 먹는 편이에요.
examples.en: I tend to make sure I eat breakfast.

examples.ko: 이 지역의 출산율은 전국 평균에 비해 높은 편이다.
examples.en: The birth rate here is relatively high compared with the national average.

cloze.en: I'm the type who makes sure to eat breakfast.

nearMiss.hint: For a habit, use present -는 편이다: 먹는 편이에요.

cloze.en: This neighborhood is fairly quiet at night.

nearMiss.hint: Adjectives take -(으)ㄴ: 조용한 편이에요.

cloze.en: I did fairly well on the exam, better than I expected.

nearMiss.hint: This rates one exam you already took: past modifier 본 편이에요.

cloze.en: This winter is relatively less cold than last year.

nearMiss.hint: ㅂ-irregular: 추운 편이에요.

cloze.en: As a student, I hardly ever skipped class.

nearMiss.hint: A past habit keeps -는 and puts the tense on 이다: 빠지는 편이었어요.

cloze.en: I know this field fairly well, too.

nearMiss.hint: ㄹ drops before -는: 아는 편이에요.

cloze.sentence: 이 지역의 출산율은 전국 평균에 비해 {{}}.

nuance.situation: 면접관이 성격을 물어요. 겸손하게 "꼼꼼하다"고 말하려면? (A modest self-description in an interview.)

options.why: -(으)ㄴ 편이다 hedges the self-description: modest but clear.
Adjectives take -(으)ㄴ 편이다; -는 is for verbs.
-(으)ㄴ/는 셈이다 means "it works out to" after weighing facts; it doesn't describe a trait.

nuance.situation: 어느 문장이 자연스러워요? (Which sentence is natural?)

options.why: Eating isn't on a scale here: without a degree word (많이, 빨리, 자주), the "tendency" has nothing to measure.
빨리 gives the scale, so "I tend to eat fast" works.

meaning: on the way (to/from) …; (be) on one's way …
nuance: Works with movement verbs: 가다, 오다, 나가다, 들어가다, 돌아오다, 내려오다, 출근하다, 퇴근하다. 공부하는 길에 makes no sense. -는 길에 introduces something done en route; -는 길이다 says where you're headed right now (지금 집에 가는 길이야). For an en-route event it stays -는 even in past narration (학교에 오는 길에 만났다). 온 길에 is a different idea ("since I came all this way"), close to -(으)ㄴ 김에. See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 113.

contrasts.note: -는 김에 is "while (I'm) at it" with any action; -는 길에 is strictly "en route".

examples.ko: 퇴근하는 길에 마트에 들러서 우유 좀 사 올래?
examples.en: Could you stop by the store on your way home from work and pick up some milk?

examples.ko: 지금 회사에서 집에 가는 길이에요.
examples.en: I'm on my way home from the office now.

cloze.sentence: {{}} 마트에 들러서 우유 좀 사 올래?
cloze.en: Could you stop by the store on your way home from work and get some milk?

nearMiss.hint: En route, keep -는: 퇴근하는 길에.
Close: -는 김에 means "while you're at it". For "on the way", the cue asks for -는 길에.

cloze.en: I'm on my way home from the office now.

nearMiss.hint: 길이다 needs 이다: 가는 길이에요.

cloze.en: On my way to school I ran into my old teacher.

nearMiss.hint: For something that happened en route use -는 길에: 오는 길에. (온 길에 means "since I came all this way".)

cloze.en: Traffic was bad on the way back from the airport.
I sprained my ankle on the way down the mountain.
Hang on, I'm just heading out.
The president is just going into a meeting.

nearMiss.hint: Keep the honorific -시- for 사장님: 들어가시는 길이에요.

cloze.en: I got soaked walking home.

nuance.situation: 어느 문장이 자연스러워요? (Which sentence is natural?)

options.why: 공부하다 isn't a trip; -는 길에 needs a movement verb.
가다 is movement, so "on the way to the library" works.

nuance.situation: 친구가 전화로 "어디야?"라고 물어요. 지금 집으로 가고 있어요. (You're heading home right now.)

options.why: -는 길이다 = "I'm on my way (there) right now."
김 only works as -는 김에 ("while I'm at it"); it can't end a sentence with 이다.
The past modifier doesn't describe being en route; use 가는 길이야.

meaning: while (I'm) at it; since (I'm) already …, (I'll also) … (using an occasion for a second action)
nuance: The first action creates an opportunity, and the second is tacked on because it's convenient. Use -는 김에 when the first action is under way or about to happen, and -(으)ㄴ 김에 when it's done and you're making use of it (부산까지 온 김에). Set phrases: 말이 나온 김에 ("since we're on the subject"), 생각난 김에. The second action is chosen, often a plan, offer, or request (나가는 김에 이것 좀 버려 줄래?); accidents don't fit (넘어졌다). Unlike -는 길에, no movement is needed (청소하는 김에 창문도 닦았다). See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 114.

contrasts.note: -는 길에 needs travel; -는 김에 takes any action that opens an opportunity.
-는 바람에 reports an unexpected cause with an unwanted result; -는 김에 is a deliberate add-on.

examples.ko: 편의점에 가는 김에 내 것도 하나 사다 줄래?
examples.en: Since you're going to the convenience store, could you get me one too?

examples.ko: 부산까지 온 김에 바다도 보고 가자.
examples.en: Since we've come all the way to Busan, let's see the ocean before we go.

cloze.sentence: 편의점에 {{}} 내 것도 하나 사다 줄래?

nearMiss.hint: Also natural for an errand on the way; the cue asks for -는 김에 ("since you're going anyway").

nearMiss.hint: The topic has already come up: past modifier 나온 김에 (a set phrase).

cloze.en: Since we've come all the way to Busan, let's see the ocean too.

nearMiss.hint: You're already here: 온 김에.

cloze.en: While I'm cleaning the room, I should wipe the windows too.

nearMiss.hint: The thought has already come to mind: 생각난 김에.

cloze.en: Since we're making bread, let's make some cookies too.

cloze.sentence: 커피 {{}} 내 것도 한 잔 부탁해.

nearMiss.hint: Keep the honorific -시- for 선생님: 나가시는 김에.

nuance.situation: 어느 문장이 자연스러워요? (Which sentence is natural?)

options.why: -는 김에 needs a second action you choose to do; tripping is an accident (use -다가).
Taking out the trash is a deliberate add-on to the trip.

nuance.situation: 집에서 대청소를 하다가 오래된 책들도 정리했어요. (While deep-cleaning, you also sorted old books.)

options.why: Cleaning gave the occasion; no travel is needed.
-는 길에 is for trips (가다, 오다…); cleaning isn't movement.
-는 바람에 reports an unexpected cause with an unwanted result; sorting the books was your choice.

meaning: I should have …; I wish I had … (wistful regret over one's own choice)
nuance: Regret about the speaker's own past choice (or "we"), often half muttered to oneself, with falling intonation. -(으)ㄹ걸 is one ending, written attached (할걸 그랬다; 할 걸 is a spacing error here). For negative regret use -지 말걸 (안 -(으)ㄹ걸 also occurs in speech). Politeness goes on 그랬다: 할걸 그랬어요. Plain 할걸요 means something else, a guess ("I bet …"). It is wistful rather than critical. To blame someone, or for a firmer "ought to have", use -았/었어야 했다 / -았/었어야지. See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 115.

contrasts.note: -았/었어야 했다 is firmer and can reproach others; -(으)ㄹ걸 그랬다 is wistful and mostly self-directed.
-(으)ㄹ걸요 (rising, conjecture) looks the same in 반말 but means "I bet …".

examples.ko: 비가 올 줄 알았으면 우산을 챙길걸 그랬어.
examples.en: If I'd known it would rain, I'd have brought an umbrella.

examples.ko: 표가 다 팔렸네요. 미리 예매할걸 그랬어요.
examples.en: They're sold out. I should have booked ahead.

cloze.en: If I'd known it would rain, I'd have brought an umbrella.

nearMiss.hint: Also "should have", but firmer; the cue asks for the wistful -(으)ㄹ걸 그랬다.

cloze.en: I shouldn't have said that yesterday.

nearMiss.hint: Also heard; the cue asks for -지 말걸, the standard negative.

cloze.en: If I'd known it was this good, I'd have ordered more.
I'm starving. I should have eaten more at lunch.

cloze.sentence: 방이 이렇게 답답할 줄 알았으면 창문을 미리 {{}}.
cloze.en: If I'd known the room would be this stuffy, I'd have opened the window earlier.

nearMiss.hint: ㄹ-stems take -ㄹ걸 directly: 열걸.

cloze.sentence: 결국 이렇게 될 줄 알았으면 선배 말을 {{}}.
cloze.en: If I'd known it would end like this, I'd have listened to my senior.

nearMiss.hint: ㄷ-irregular: 들을걸.

cloze.en: I should have helped my friend back then.

nearMiss.hint: ㅂ-irregular: 도울걸.

cloze.en: They're sold out. I should have booked ahead.

nearMiss.hint: In 해요체, -(으)ㄹ걸요 alone is a guess ("I bet …"); for regret say 예매할걸 그랬어요.

nuance.situation: 동생이 또 지각했어요. 동생을 나무라며 "좀 일찍 나왔어야지"라는 뜻을 전하려면? (You want to scold your sibling for being late.)

options.why: -았/었어야지 carries the reproach you want.
-(으)ㄹ걸 그랬다 is wistful regret, mostly about the speaker's own choices; it doesn't scold.

nuance.situation: 시험이 끝나고 혼잣말로 아쉬워해요. (After the exam, you mutter a regret to yourself.)

options.why: Regret over your own choice, muttered to yourself.
-(으)ㄹ걸요 is a guess ("I bet they'll study more"); it doesn't express regret.

features.label: Keep 그랬- (있을걸요 alone would be a guess, not regret)

meaning: with … still …; in the state of having … (a resulting state kept during the next action)
nuance: The first action is complete and its resulting state carries over while the main action happens, often implying it shouldn't have: 불을 켠 채로 잠들었다. It always uses the past modifier -(으)ㄴ (켜는 채로 is wrong). It's typical with state-creating verbs (입다, 신다, 쓰다, 켜다, 열다, 앉다, 눕다) and negatives (하지 않은 채). 채 is a dependent noun, so it is spaced (신은 채로). Don't confuse it with the adverb 채 ("not even": 채 1분도 안 돼서) or the suffix -째 ("whole": 껍질째). See also HowtoStudyKorean Lesson 116.

contrasts.note: -아/어 놓다 leaves a result in place on purpose; -(으)ㄴ 채로 describes doing something else while that state lasts.
-(으)ㄴ 김에 uses a finished action as an opportunity; -(으)ㄴ 채로 just keeps its state.

examples.ko: 어젯밤에 불을 켠 채로 잠들어 버렸어요.
examples.en: Last night I fell asleep with the light on.

examples.ko: 그 사건은 범인을 찾지 못한 채 미제 사건으로 남았다.
examples.en: The case remained unsolved, the culprit never found.

cloze.en: Last night I fell asleep with the light on.

nearMiss.hint: Always the past modifier: 켠 채로.

cloze.en: You can't come into the room with your shoes on.

nearMiss.hint: Always the past modifier: 신은 채로.

cloze.en: I went out with the window open.

nearMiss.hint: ㄹ-stems drop ㄹ before -ㄴ: 연 채로.

cloze.en: He left without saying a word.

nearMiss.hint: ㅂ-irregular: 누운 채로.

nearMiss.hint: Always the past modifier: 쓴 채로.

nuance.situation: 어느 문장이 맞아요? (Which sentence is correct?)

options.why: The completed state (clothes on) is kept: 입은 채로.
-(으)ㄴ 채로 needs the completed state: 입은, not 입는.
-째 means "whole, including" (껍질째); the state noun is 채.

nuance.situation: "He left with the door open"을 옮기려면? (Translate the sentence.)

options.why: The door stays open as he leaves: -(으)ㄴ 채로.
-(으)ㄴ 김에 means "since he'd already opened it, he (also) left"; it doesn't say the door stayed open.
